source.title: The Clock and the Pizza: Two Stories in Mechanistic Explanation of Neural Networks
source.authors: Ziqian Zhong; Zi-Ming Liu; Max Tegmark; Jacob Andreas

record.tranche_reason: The study trains modular-addition networks and reports that networks on the same task can implement different algorithms, with the algorithm depending on architecture and hyperparameters. This challenges V6.
record.gate_note: The paper cites the original grokking and progress-measures studies, but does not test grokking’s delayed-generalization trajectory or vary training-set size. Its main results concern algorithm identity in modular addition. The training-dynamics observations and non-circular-model rates are recorded as findings that do not test a listed version.
record.test_reason: The study trains many modular-addition networks (p=59) and classifies their learned algorithms. Its own results show Clock, Pizza, hybrid and non-circular solutions depending on attention rate, width, depth and architecture. This bears directly on V6. It does not track a delayed-generalization trajectory: it uses an 80% train split, AdamW with weight decay 2, and 20k full-batch epochs, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that familiar algorithm discovery in modular addition is not inevitable. Clock, Pizza and more complex or non-circular procedures arise depending on the relative strength of attention vs linear layers (and on width, depth and seeds), and networks sometimes ensemble several copies in parallel.
record.recipe_differences: This is a modular-addition algorithm-characterization study, not a reproduction of the grokking training-trajectory experiment or the progress-measures method. Its main transformer setup uses p=59, an 80% training and 20% validation split, and algorithm-classification measures such as gradient symmetricity and distance irrelevance.
record.method_sensitivity: Algorithmic phase changes with attention rate and width; the phase-change point increases with width. The paper also reports different behaviors across model architectures and layer counts.

fits_no_version.finding: Pizza-like logit patterns appear early in a Clock (attention rate 1) run and then dissolve.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Algorithm identity can shift during training, independently of any grokking delay.

fits_no_version.finding: An accompanying-Pizza circle appears early in constant-attention training. Removing it costs 99.7% to 97.9% accuracy early, but almost nothing in the trained model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some auxiliary circuits form early and lose functional importance later.

record.problems: The study focuses on one task, modular addition mod p=59. Main phase-space plots include runs reaching 100% validation accuracy, and most displayed outcomes are described qualitatively rather than with uncertainty estimates. The paper itself notes that its techniques need further work before scaling to real-world models.
record.rows_left_out: No additional plotted run-level values were extracted where the text did not state a value or provide an unambiguous mapping. Figure 10 reports that 34.31% of all trained one-layer transformer runs are circular, but does not identify their algorithm; the algorithmic classification plots in Figures 7, 10, 11, 14, 18, 19, and 21 contain additional points whose individual values are not stated in the text.

untested.parts: Tasks other than modular addition. Groups or operations beyond p=59. Seed-only variation at fixed hyperparameters is not quantified as a rate.
All parts: there are no train/test accuracy curves, no measured delay, and no variation of training-set size.
All parts. Appendix J/K show Pizza or accompanying-Pizza patterns early in training, but no progress measure is tied to a generalization jump.
All parts: only algorithmic data is used, and initialization scale is not manipulated.
All parts. Pruning under weight decay is only a conjecture (Section 3.4).

missing.what: Robustness variations (GeLU activation, separate embeddings for the two tokens, added equal-sign token) still show both Pizza and Clock and the phase change.
34.31% of all one-layer transformer runs are circular; the rest are non-circular algorithms (declared in rows_left_out but relevant to V6).
Accompanying-pizza formula FVE of 97.2–97.7% for circles #4–#6 in Model A.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Training uses an 80% data fraction with heavy weight decay, and runs below 100% validation accuracy were removed, so the phase plots are conditioned on successful runs. Most phase-space results are only plotted; no uncertainty is reported. Model B reproduces Nanda et al.'s Clock, so the Clock finding replicates in its own regime, but the claim of a single convergent algorithm does not hold across settings.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not track training and test accuracy over time, establish a long delay after training accuracy saturates, or vary training-set size.

It observes algorithmic patterns during training, but does not test whether a generalizing circuit gradually forms before a grokking jump, whether memorizing components are removed after overfitting, or whether progress measures anticipate such a jump.
The experiments use algorithmic modular addition, not non-algorithmic data such as images, text, or molecules; they do not test initialization scale or a lazy-to-rich transition.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is studied.
The study does not test whether low-norm circuits are more efficient, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking. Its discussion of pruning with weight decay is a conjecture.
The study tests modular addition with its reported architectures and hyperparameters, not whether the result holds across all tasks, architectures, or training regimes.
It does not test whether optimizer or numerical artifacts produce the delays described in V7.

relationships.condition: One-layer transformers on mod-59 addition, varying attention rate and width
relationships.reason: The constant-attention model implements Pizza and the standard-attention model implements Clock (r1–r10). A sharp Pizza-to-Clock phase boundary shifts with width (r14, r15). Pizza appears even at attention rate 1 at width 1024 (r19, r20).
relationships.display_finding: Constant attention produced Pizza and standard attention produced Clock, with a width-dependent phase boundary and Pizza appearing even at attention rate 1 with width 1024.
